stem: What does `git add notes.txt` do?

options.text: Copies the file's current content into the staging area (index)
options.why: The index holds the snapshot the next commit will record; `add` updates it with what is on disk now.

options.text: Creates a new commit that contains only `notes.txt`
options.why: Commits are made by `git commit`; `add` only prepares what the commit will contain.

options.text: Uploads the file to the remote repository straight away
options.why: Nothing leaves your machine until you push; `add` is a purely local operation.

options.text: Marks the file so that every later edit to it is included automatically
options.why: The index stores a copy of the content at that moment; later edits must be added again.

explanation: Git has three areas: the working tree (your files), the index or staging area (the proposed next commit), and the repository (committed history). `git add` copies the file's current content into the index. If you edit the file again, the index still holds the earlier version until you run `git add` again.
reference: Pro Git: Recording Changes to the Repository

stem: Conceptually, Git records each commit as a snapshot of the whole project, storing unchanged files by reference to the version it already has, rather than as a list of line-by-line changes.

options.text: True
options.why: Each commit points to a tree describing every file; unchanged files reuse the existing blob instead of being copied.

options.text: False
options.why: That delta model describes tools like SVN; Git's data model is snapshots, and compression into packfiles is a separate storage detail.

explanation: Git thinks of history as a series of snapshots. A commit points to a tree for the whole project, and files that did not change reuse the same blob object. Git does compress objects into packfiles with deltas, but that is a storage optimisation, not how history is modelled.

stem: A file was committed by mistake. You want Git to stop tracking it but keep the file on your disk. Complete the command: `____ .env` (type the command and its option).
explanation: `git rm --cached <file>` removes the file from the index, so the next commit records its deletion, but it leaves the file in your working tree. Plain `git rm` would delete it from disk too. Add the file to `.gitignore` as well so it is not added again by accident.

stem: Git is a distributed version control system. What does that mean for a normal `git clone`?

options.text: Only the latest snapshot is copied, and history stays on the server
options.why: That describes a centralised checkout; a normal Git clone copies the full history.

options.text: The clone has the full history, so you can commit and read logs offline
options.why: Every clone is a full repository; only push and fetch need the network.

options.text: Each developer stores a different subset of the files in the project
options.why: All clones contain the same project; "distributed" refers to history, not to sharding files.

options.text: Commits are sent automatically to every other clone as soon as you make them
options.why: Nothing is shared until you push or someone fetches; commits are local first.

explanation: In a centralised system such as SVN, the history lives on one server and you check out a working copy. In Git every clone is a complete repository with full history. You can commit, branch, diff and read logs offline, and you exchange commits explicitly with fetch, pull and push.

stem: Match each `git status --short` line with what it means. (The first column is the staging area, the second the working tree.)

options.text: A new file that is not tracked yet
A new file whose content is staged
A tracked file changed but not staged
A tracked file whose deletion is staged

explanation: The short format has two columns: X is the index (staged) state and Y is the working-tree state. `??` means untracked, `A ` means added to the index, ` M` means modified in the working tree only, and `D ` means the deletion has been staged.

stem: You want every new repository you create with `git init` to start on a branch called `main`. Which setting does this?

options.text: `git config --global init.defaultBranch main`
options.why: This is the setting `git init` reads when naming the first branch.

options.text: `git config --global core.defaultBranchName main`
options.why: There is no `core.mainBranch` option; Git would simply ignore it.

options.text: `git config --global branch.default main`
options.why: This key does not exist; branch defaults live under `init.defaultBranch`.

options.text: `git config --global remote.origin.head main`
options.why: That would only describe a remote; it does not affect what `git init` creates.

explanation: `init.defaultBranch` sets the name of the initial branch for repositories created with `git init`. You can also pass `git init -b main` for a single repository. A clone uses whatever branch the remote's HEAD points to instead.

stem: Which statements about `.gitignore` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It only affects files that are not tracked yet
options.why: Ignore rules stop untracked files from being added; files already tracked are not affected.

options.text: A `.gitignore` in a subdirectory applies to paths under that directory
options.why: Patterns are relative to the directory the `.gitignore` lives in.

options.text: It removes matching files from earlier commits in the history
options.why: Ignore rules never touch history; rewriting history is a separate, deliberate step.

options.text: It must be stored in `.git/` so that it is shared with the team
options.why: `.gitignore` is a normal committed file; `.git/info/exclude` is the private, unshared one.

options.text: It makes Git delete matching files from your working tree
options.why: Ignored files stay on disk; Git just stops offering them as untracked.

explanation: `.gitignore` tells Git which untracked files to leave alone. It does not affect tracked files, does not delete anything, and does not change history. You can place `.gitignore` files in subdirectories; their patterns are relative to that directory.

stem: Put the things `git clone https://example.com/app.git` does in order.

options.text: Creates an `app` directory with a new `.git` repository inside
Adds a remote called `origin` pointing at the URL
Fetches all the commits and branches from the remote
Checks out the remote's default branch into the working tree

explanation: `git clone` is roughly `git init`, then `git remote add origin <url>`, then `git fetch`, then a checkout of the branch the remote's HEAD points to (creating a local branch that tracks it). The other branches are available as remote-tracking branches such as `origin/feature`.

stem:
In a new repository you run:

```bash
echo a > f.txt
git add f.txt
echo b >> f.txt
git status --short
```

What does the last command print?

options.text: `A  f.txt`
options.why: That would mean the working tree matches the index, but the file was edited after `git add`.

options.text: `AM f.txt`
options.why: The first column shows the file staged as new; the second shows it modified in the working tree since then.

options.text: `?? f.txt`
options.why: The file is tracked once it has been added; `??` is only for untracked files.

options.text: `MM f.txt`
options.why: The first column can't be M: the file has never been committed, so it is a new addition.

explanation: The first column compares the index with HEAD; the file is new there, so it shows `A`. The second column compares the working tree with the index; the file gained a line after `git add`, so it shows `M`. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: Continuing from `echo a > f.txt`, `git add f.txt`, `echo b >> f.txt`, you now run `git commit -m one` (no `-a`). What does `f.txt` contain in that commit?

options.text: Only the line `a`
options.why: A commit records the index, and the index still holds the content from the `git add`.

options.text: The two lines `a` and `b`
options.why: The second line was never staged, so it stays as a working-tree change.

options.text: Nothing, because the commit is rejected
options.why: Git commits the staged snapshot happily; unstaged edits don't block it.

options.text: Only the second line, `b`
options.why: The index has the version from the moment of `git add`, which is just `a`.

explanation: `git commit` records exactly what is in the index. The index got the one-line version at `git add` time, so the commit contains only `a`. Afterwards `git status --short` shows ` M f.txt`, because the line `b` is still only in the working tree. Verified with Git 2.55.
reference: Pro Git: Recording Changes to the Repository

stem: You edit the tracked file `app.js` and create a new file `util.js`, then run `git commit -am "update"`. What happens?

options.text: Both files are committed, because `-a` stages every change in the folder
options.why: `-a` only covers files Git already tracks, so a brand-new file is skipped.

options.text: The change to `app.js` is committed and `util.js` stays untracked
options.why: `-a` stages modified and deleted tracked files, never untracked ones.

options.text: The commit fails until `util.js` is added or ignored
options.why: Untracked files never block a commit; they are just left out of it.

options.text: Only `util.js` is committed, because it is the newest file
options.why: Newness doesn't matter; untracked files are exactly what `-a` skips.

explanation: `git commit -a` automatically stages files that are already tracked and have been modified or deleted, then commits. It does not add untracked files, so `util.js` remains `??` until you run `git add util.js`. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: `.env` was committed months ago. You add a line `.env` to `.gitignore` and then edit `.env`. What does `git status --short` show for `.env`?

options.text: Nothing: the file now matches a rule, so Git hides all of its changes
options.why: Ignore rules only apply to untracked files, and `.env` is still tracked.

options.text: ` M .env`, because the file is still tracked despite the new rule
options.why: Tracked files keep being tracked; you must untrack it with `git rm --cached`.

options.text: `!! .env`, which marks a tracked file as ignored and modified
options.why: `!!` only appears with `--ignored`, and only for untracked ignored files.

options.text: `D  .env`, because ignoring a tracked file stages its removal
options.why: Git never stages anything on its own when you edit `.gitignore`.

explanation: `.gitignore` has no effect on files that are already in the index. Git keeps tracking `.env` and reports its modification. To stop tracking it, run `git rm --cached .env` and commit. Because the file is still in older commits, rotate any secrets it held. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: Since the last commit you renamed `a.txt` to `b.txt` with plain `mv`, deleted `del.txt`, edited `keep.txt` and created `untracked.txt`. You run `git add -u`. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The deletion of `del.txt` is staged
options.why: `-u` stages modifications and deletions of tracked files.

options.text: `untracked.txt` is still untracked
options.why: `-u` never adds new files; `git add -A` would.

options.text: The rename is staged as `R  a.txt -> b.txt`
options.why: `b.txt` is a new, untracked file, so `-u` stages only the deletion of `a.txt`.

options.text: `untracked.txt` is staged as a new file
options.why: Only `git add -A` or an explicit path would stage it.

options.text: The edit to `keep.txt` stays unstaged
options.why: Modified tracked files are exactly what `-u` stages.

explanation: `git add -u` updates the index for files Git already tracks: modifications and deletions. New files, including `b.txt`, are left untracked, so the rename shows up as `D  a.txt` plus `?? b.txt`. `git add -A` stages everything, and status then shows `R  a.txt -> b.txt` and `A  untracked.txt`. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: Git reads configuration from several places. Order them from LOWEST to HIGHEST priority (later values override earlier ones).

options.text: System config (for all users on the machine)
Global config (your user, `~/.gitconfig`)
Local config (this repository, `.git/config`)
A `-c name=value` option on the command line

explanation: Git reads system, then global, then local (and worktree, if enabled) config, so more specific files win. A `-c name=value` on the command line overrides all of them for that single command. With Git 2.55, a repository with `user.name=LocalName` still reports `CmdName` when run as `git -c user.name=CmdName config user.name`.

stem: If you create an empty directory `logs/` and run `git add -A`, Git starts tracking the directory, so collaborators get an empty `logs/` folder when they clone.

options.text: True
options.why: Git only tracks file content; a directory exists in a commit only if it contains a tracked file.

options.text: False
options.why: Git doesn't record empty directories, so teams add a placeholder file such as `.gitkeep`.

explanation: Git's trees record files, and directories appear only as the paths of those files. An empty directory has nothing to record, so `git status` and `git add` ignore it. The usual workaround is a placeholder file such as `.gitkeep` (a convention, not a Git feature). Verified with Git 2.55.
reference: Git FAQ: Can I add empty directories?

stem:
In a repository, `git config --show-origin --get user.name` prints:

```
file:.git/config	LocalName
```

What does this tell you?

options.text: The value comes from the repository's own config, which beats global
options.why: Local config is read after global, so its value wins for this repository.

options.text: Your global config has no `user.name`, so Git fell back to the local file
options.why: Local wins regardless; the global file may well set a different name.

options.text: The name will be used for all repositories on this machine
options.why: `.git/config` belongs to this repository only.

options.text: Commits will be rejected until the global name matches
options.why: Git never compares levels; it simply uses the highest-priority value.

explanation: `--show-origin` prints the file each value came from. `.git/config` is the local level, which overrides the global and system files for this repository. `--show-scope` prints the level name (`local`) instead. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: You stage a brand-new file `new.txt` with `git add`, then delete it from disk without telling Git. Type the two-character code `git status --short` shows for it.
explanation: The index still contains the staged new file (A in the first column), and the working tree no longer has it (D in the second column), so the line is `AD new.txt`. Committing now would add the staged content even though the file is gone from disk. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: You change the tracked file `f.txt` without staging it, then run `git rm f.txt`. What happens?

options.text: The file is deleted and the deletion is staged, silently losing your edits
options.why: Git protects uncommitted work and refuses instead of discarding it.

options.text: Git refuses because of local modifications, suggesting `--cached` or `-f`
options.why: It won't remove a file whose changes would be lost without one of those flags.

options.text: Only the index entry is removed, and the file stays on disk
options.why: That is what `--cached` does; plain `git rm` also deletes the working-tree file.

options.text: Git stages your edits first, then stages the deletion
options.why: Git never stages changes on your behalf before removing a file.

explanation: `git rm` deletes the file from the working tree and stages the removal, but only if that wouldn't throw away uncommitted changes. Git 2.55 prints "error: the following file has local modifications … (use --cached to keep the file, or -f to force removal)".

stem: You run `git mv app.txt main.txt`. What does `git status --short` show?

options.text: `D  app.txt` and `?? main.txt`
options.why: That is what plain `mv` leaves before staging; `git mv` stages both sides.

options.text: `R  app.txt -> main.txt`
options.why: `git mv` stages the deletion and the addition, and status detects the rename.

options.text: `RM main.txt`
options.why: Nothing changed after the move, so the working-tree column is empty.

options.text: `M  main.txt`
options.why: A rename isn't a modification of an existing path; the old path disappears.

explanation: `git mv` is a convenience: it renames the file and stages the result. Git doesn't store renames; `status`, `diff` and `log` detect them by comparing content. Running `mv` then `git add -A` gives the same `R  app.txt -> main.txt`. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem:
`.gitignore` contains:

```
logs/
!logs/keep.txt
```

`logs/keep.txt` and `logs/a.log` both exist and are untracked. What does `git status --untracked-files=all` list?

options.text: `logs/keep.txt` only, because the negation re-includes it
options.why: A negation can't re-include a file when its parent directory is excluded.

options.text: Neither file, because Git never looks inside the ignored `logs/` directory
options.why: Excluding the directory hides everything below it, so the negation never applies.

options.text: Both files, because a negation cancels the whole `logs/` rule
options.why: A negation only targets the paths it matches; it doesn't cancel other patterns.

options.text: `logs/a.log` only, because a negation inverts the pattern on the line before it
options.why: Negations don't invert other rules; they un-ignore the paths they match.

explanation: The gitignore docs say it is not possible to re-include a file if a parent directory of that file is excluded, because Git doesn't list excluded directories for performance. `git check-ignore -v logs/keep.txt` reports `.gitignore:1:logs/`. To keep one file, ignore the directory's contents instead: `logs/*` then `!logs/keep.txt`. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: You want to ignore everything in `logs/` except `logs/keep.txt`. Which `.gitignore` works?

options.text: `logs/*` followed by `!logs/keep.txt`
options.why: Ignoring the contents (not the directory) lets Git look inside, so the negation applies.

options.text: `logs/` followed by `!logs/keep.txt`
options.why: Excluding the directory itself stops Git looking inside, so the file stays ignored.

options.text: `!logs/keep.txt` first, followed by `logs/`
options.why: The directory rule still excludes `logs/` entirely, so the negation never applies.

options.text: `logs/**/!keep.txt` on a single line
options.why: `!` only means negation at the start of a pattern; here it would be matched literally.

explanation: `logs/*` ignores the entries inside `logs/` but not the directory itself, so Git still scans it and can apply `!logs/keep.txt`. With this file, Git 2.55 lists `?? logs/keep.txt` while `logs/a.log` stays ignored.

stem: The root `.gitignore` has the line `/build/`. Untracked files exist at `build/y.o` and `src/build/x.o`. Which file does `git status` still offer as untracked?

options.text: `src/build/x.o`, because a leading slash anchors the pattern to the root
options.why: `/build/` matches only the top-level `build` directory.

options.text: `build/y.o`, because a leading slash makes the pattern match nested paths only
options.why: It is the other way round: the leading slash restricts matching to the root.

options.text: Neither, because `build/` directories are ignored at any depth
options.why: That is true of `build/` without the leading slash.

options.text: Both, because the trailing slash only matches files named `build`
options.why: A trailing slash means the pattern matches directories, not files.

explanation: A slash at the start or in the middle of a pattern makes it relative to the `.gitignore`'s directory, so `/build/` means only the top-level build directory. A pattern with only a trailing slash, `build/`, matches a directory with that name at any depth. Verified with Git 2.55: `src/build/x.o` stayed untracked with `/build/`, and was ignored with `build/`.

stem: You want Git to ignore your personal `notes.local` file without adding any rule that your teammates would receive. Which mechanisms do that? (Choose two.)

options.text: A pattern in `.git/info/exclude` of this repository
options.why: That file is inside `.git/`, so it is never committed or shared.

options.text: A pattern in your global excludes file (`core.excludesFile`)
options.why: The global excludes file applies to all your repositories and stays on your machine.

options.text: A pattern in the repository's root `.gitignore`
options.why: Root `.gitignore` is usually committed, so teammates would receive the rule.

options.text: An `export-ignore` attribute in `.gitattributes`
options.why: That only affects `git archive` output, not untracked-file listings.

options.text: Running `git rm --cached notes.local` once
options.why: The file was never tracked, and untracking doesn't ignore anything anyway.

explanation: Git reads ignore rules from `.gitignore` files (normally committed), from `.git/info/exclude` (per repository, never shared) and from the file set in `core.excludesFile` (per user, default `~/.config/git/ignore`). For personal files such as editor droppings or local notes, use one of the last two. Git 2.55 reports the source with `git check-ignore -v`, for example `.git/info/exclude:7:notes.local`.

stem:
You run `git check-ignore -v logs/keep.txt` and get:

```
.gitignore:1:logs/	logs/keep.txt
```

What does this tell you?

options.text: The file is tracked even though line 1 of `.gitignore` matches it
options.why: `check-ignore` reports ignore matches; it says nothing about tracking.

options.text: Line 1 of the root `.gitignore`, the pattern `logs/`, is what ignores the file
options.why: `-v` prints the source file, line number and pattern that decided the result.

options.text: The file is ignored only because the `.gitignore` file has a syntax error on line 1
options.why: There is no error; `logs/` is a valid directory pattern.

options.text: The negation on line 1 re-includes the file into Git's listings
options.why: The pattern shown, `logs/`, has no leading `!`, so it isn't a negation.

explanation: `git check-ignore -v` is the quickest way to debug ignore rules. It prints `<source>:<line>:<pattern>` followed by a tab and the path. Here it shows the directory rule `logs/` winning over any later `!logs/keep.txt`, because Git never looks inside an excluded directory.

stem: `.gitignore` contains `build/` (no leading slash). `src/build/x.o` is the only file under `src/`. What does `git status --short --ignored` show for it?

options.text: `?? src/build/x.o`, because the pattern only matches at the root
options.why: Without a leading slash, `build/` matches a `build` directory at any depth.

options.text: `!! src/`, because everything inside `src/` is ignored
options.why: Status collapses a directory whose contents are all ignored into one `!!` entry.

options.text: `!! src/build/x.o`, listing the individual ignored file
options.why: In the default (non-`all`) mode, status shows the highest fully ignored directory instead.

options.text: Nothing, because `--ignored` hides ignored files
options.why: `--ignored` does the opposite: it adds ignored entries, marked `!!`.

explanation: A pattern with only a trailing slash matches a directory of that name anywhere, so `src/build/` is ignored. Because `src/` contains nothing else, `git status --ignored` reports `!! src/`. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: A repository at `../repo` has two commits on `main` and a `feature` branch. You run `git clone --depth 1 ../repo copy`. What do you get?

options.text: A shallow clone with one commit and both branches
options.why: `--depth` is ignored for a plain local path, so the clone isn't shallow.

options.text: A warning that `--depth` is ignored; full `main` history, no `origin/feature`
options.why: Local-path clones ignore depth, but `--depth` still implies single-branch.

options.text: An error, because shallow clones need a network URL
options.why: Git doesn't fail; it warns and carries on with a full, local clone.

options.text: A shallow clone containing one commit and only `origin/main`, as you asked for
options.why: You get that with `file:///…/repo`; a plain path ignores `--depth`.

explanation: For a plain local path, Git clones by hard-linking objects and prints "warning: --depth is ignored in local clones; use file:// instead.", so `main` keeps both commits. `--depth` still implies `--single-branch`, so only `origin/main` is created. With `file:///…/repo` the same command produces a real shallow clone: `rev-list --count HEAD` is 1 and `rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` is true. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem:
You rename `big.txt` to `huge.txt` with plain `mv`, then replace three of its four lines, and run `git add -A`. Status shows:

```
D  big.txt
A  huge.txt
```

Why isn't it shown as a rename?

options.text: Git can only detect renames that were made with `git mv`, never with plain `mv`
options.why: `git mv` and `mv` + `add -A` produce the same index; detection is content-based.

options.text: Too little content is shared, so it falls under the 50% similarity threshold
options.why: Git infers renames by comparing content; heavily edited files look like new ones.

options.text: Renames are only detected after the change has been committed
options.why: Status detects renames in the index too, as `R  a.txt -> b.txt` shows.

options.text: Rename detection is turned off by default in `git status`
options.why: It is on by default; an unchanged rename appears as `R`.

explanation: Git doesn't record renames. `status`, `diff` and `log` infer them by pairing a deleted path with an added path whose content is similar enough, 50% by default (`-M`). Only one of four lines survived, so Git reports a deletion and an addition. Rename and edit in separate commits if you want history to follow the file. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: Match each configuration level with where Git keeps it by default (on Linux).

options.text: `/etc/gitconfig` (or the Git install's `etc/gitconfig`)
`~/.gitconfig` or `~/.config/git/config`
`.git/config` in the repository
`.git/config.worktree`, when `extensions.worktreeConfig` is on

explanation: `--system` applies to every user, `--global` to your user, `--local` to one repository, and `--worktree` to one linked worktree when `extensions.worktreeConfig` is enabled (otherwise it behaves like `--local`). Later levels override earlier ones. `git config --list --show-origin` shows which file each value came from.

stem: Which of these can a `.gitattributes` file control? (Choose three.)

options.text: Forcing LF line endings on checkout for `*.sh` with `text eol=lf`
options.why: `eol` sets the working-tree line ending regardless of the user's settings.

options.text: Treating `*.png` as `binary`, so no text diffs or line-ending changes
options.why: `binary` is a macro for `-diff -merge -text`.

options.text: Leaving `tests/` out of `git archive` with `export-ignore`
options.why: Paths with `export-ignore` are skipped when building archives.

options.text: Making Git ignore untracked files that match a pattern
options.why: That is `.gitignore`'s job; attributes don't affect untracked-file listings.

options.text: Encrypting the matching files before they are committed
options.why: Plain attributes do no encryption; tools like git-crypt add their own filters.

explanation: `.gitattributes` assigns attributes to paths: line-ending handling (`text`, `eol`), binary treatment, diff and merge drivers, `export-ignore` for archives, and filters such as Git LFS. Git 2.55 confirmed that `tests/ export-ignore` removed `tests/t.txt` from a `git archive` tar listing.

stem: Windows teammates use `core.autocrlf=true`, and shell scripts keep breaking with `\r` errors in Linux containers. Type the `.gitattributes` line that makes every `*.sh` file check out with LF endings for everyone.
explanation: `*.sh text eol=lf` marks the files as text and always checks them out with LF, overriding `core.autocrlf`. In a test with Git 2.55, a clone made with `core.autocrlf=true` checked out `script.sh` with `\n` endings, while an unattributed `readme.txt` got `\r\n`.

stem: A repository's `.gitattributes` says `*.sh text eol=lf`. A developer clones it with `core.autocrlf=true`. `deploy.sh` is checked out with LF line endings, while files without an attribute get CRLF.

options.text: True
options.why: The `eol` attribute takes precedence over `core.autocrlf` for the paths it matches.

options.text: False
options.why: Per-path attributes win over the global `core.autocrlf` setting; that is their purpose.

explanation:
Attributes are committed with the project, so they apply to everyone, unlike `core.autocrlf`, which each developer sets. Git 2.55 confirmed it: `od -c` showed `a 
 b 
` for the `.sh` file and `a  
 b  
` for an unattributed text file.

stem: A file goes through these states from creation to after it is edited again. Put them in order.

options.text: Untracked: it exists on disk but Git has never been told about it
Staged: `git add` copied its content into the index
Unmodified: `git commit` recorded it and the working tree matches
Modified: it was edited and differs from the last commit

explanation: A new file starts untracked. `git add` stages it, `git commit` records it, and it is then unmodified. Editing it makes it modified, and `git add` moves it back to staged. Tracked files cycle through unmodified, modified and staged; untracked files stay outside the cycle until you add them.
reference: Pro Git: Recording Changes to the Repository

stem: You fixed a bug and added debug logging in the same file. You run `git add -p app.js`, stage only the bug-fix hunk, and commit. What does `git status --short` show for `app.js` afterwards?

options.text: Nothing, because `-p` commits the whole file once you start
options.why: `-p` lets you pick hunks; the hunks you skip stay as working-tree changes.

options.text: ` M app.js`, because the debug logging is still an unstaged change
options.why: The commit took the staged hunk; the rest remains modified in the working tree.

options.text: `MM app.js`, with the debug logging staged and waiting for the next commit
options.why: You declined that hunk, so nothing about it is in the index.

options.text: `?? app.js`, because partial staging untracks the file
options.why: The file stays tracked; partial staging only affects which changes are in the index.

explanation: `git add -p` walks through each hunk and asks whether to stage it, so one file can contribute only part of its changes to a commit. After committing the staged hunk, the remaining debug lines are still a difference between the working tree and HEAD, so the file shows ` M`.

stem: An API key was committed in `.env` three commits ago and pushed to a shared remote. A teammate runs `git rm --cached .env`, adds `.env` to `.gitignore`, commits and pushes. What is the situation now?

options.text: The key is gone from the repository, because the file is no longer tracked
options.why: Untracking only affects future commits; earlier commits still contain the file.

options.text: The key is still in history and in every clone, so it must be revoked and rotated
options.why: Anyone with a clone can recover it from older commits; revoking is the only safe fix.

options.text: The key is removed from older commits as soon as the ignore rule is pushed
options.why: Pushing a `.gitignore` never rewrites existing commits.

options.text: The key is safe, because files named `.env` are excluded from every `git clone` by default
options.why: Git has no special handling for `.env`; it is cloned like any other tracked file.

explanation: Untracking and ignoring stop the file being committed again, but every existing commit, and every clone and fork made since, still has it (`git show HEAD~1:.env`). Treat a pushed secret as leaked: revoke and rotate it first. Rewriting history (for example with git filter-repo) and force-pushing is optional cleanup that can't reach copies others already have.
reference: GitHub Docs: Removing sensitive data from a repository

stem:
On Windows with `core.autocrlf=true`, `git add f.txt` prints:

```
warning: in the working copy of 'f.txt', LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches it
```

What does this mean?

options.text: The commit will contain CRLF endings for `f.txt` from now on
options.why: With `autocrlf=true` the repository stores LF; conversion happens on checkout.

options.text: Git stores LF, but the next checkout will write CRLF to the working tree
options.why: `autocrlf=true` normalises to LF in the repository and writes CRLF to the working tree.

options.text: It has already rewritten the file on disk so that it now uses CRLF line endings
options.why: Nothing has changed yet; the warning says it will happen the next time Git writes the file.

options.text: The file is binary and Git refuses to convert its line endings
options.why: The warning appears precisely because Git treats the file as text.

explanation: With `core.autocrlf=true`, Git converts CRLF to LF when adding, and LF to CRLF when checking out. A file written with LF only is stored unchanged, but the next checkout of it (switching branches, reset, a fresh clone) will produce CRLF, so Git warns you. Projects avoid this churn by committing a `.gitattributes`, for example `* text=auto` plus per-type `eol` rules. Warning text from Git 2.55.

stem: A remote has `main` (many commits) and `feature`. You run `git clone --depth 1 file:///srv/repo copy`. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git rev-list --count HEAD` prints 1 in the new clone
options.why: A depth-1 clone over `file://` contains only the tip commit.

options.text: Only `origin/main` exists, because `--depth` implies `--single-branch`
options.why: Shallow clones fetch only the default branch unless you pass `--no-single-branch`.

options.text: The clone can never get more history, so you must clone again
options.why: `git fetch --unshallow` (or `--deepen`) downloads the rest later.

options.text: `git log` still shows the full history, because only file content is truncated
options.why: Shallow clones truncate commit history, not file contents.

options.text: Both `origin/main` and `origin/feature` are present with one commit each
options.why: Without `--no-single-branch`, `feature` isn't fetched at all.

explanation: Git 2.55 confirmed it: `rev-list --count HEAD` was 1, `rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` was true, and `branch -a` showed only `main` and `origin/main`. Shallow clones speed up CI. Their limits: commands that need older history fail or behave oddly (`git describe`, `merge-base`, `blame` past the cut), and `git fetch --unshallow` repairs that.

stem: A teammate runs `git init` again inside an existing repository that already has commits. What happens?

options.text: Git prints "Reinitialized existing Git repository"; history is untouched
options.why: Re-running init is safe; it only fills in missing files such as new templates.

options.text: The repository's history is wiped and a fresh, empty repository is created
options.why: Git never deletes existing objects or refs when re-initialising.

options.text: Git refuses with an error because a `.git` directory already exists
options.why: There is no error; Git explicitly supports re-initialising.

options.text: A second, nested `.git` directory is created inside the first one
options.why: Git reuses the existing `.git`; it never nests repositories this way.

explanation: The docs say running `git init` in an existing repository is safe and won't overwrite things that are already there. It re-applies templates and can change some settings, such as `--shared`. Git 2.55 printed "Reinitialized existing Git repository in …/.git/", and `git log` still showed the earlier commit.

stem: A CI job runs `git commit` in a repository whose `.git/config` sets `user.name=LocalName`. The job runs `git -c user.name=ci-bot commit -m "release"`. Which author name is recorded?

options.text: `LocalName`, because repository config always beats command-line options
options.why: Command-line `-c` values are read last, so they override every config file.

options.text: `ci-bot`, because `-c` overrides every config file for that one command
options.why: Values passed with `-c` take precedence over the system, global and local files.

options.text: Whatever the global `~/.gitconfig` says, because CI ignores local config
options.why: CI runs ordinary Git; the local file is read, then overridden by `-c`.

options.text: The commit fails, because two different names are configured
options.why: Git just takes the highest-priority value; conflicting levels never cause an error.

explanation: Git reads system, global and local config, then applies `-c` options (and `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_n` variables) on top. With Git 2.55, `git -c user.name=CmdName config user.name` printed `CmdName` in a repository whose local config had `LocalName`. For authorship, `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` and `--author` override config too.

stem: You stage a version of `f.txt` with `git add`, edit it again, then run `git rm f.txt`. Git prints "the following file has staged content different from both the file and the HEAD … (use -f to force removal)". Why only `-f` here, and not `--cached`?

options.text: `--cached` is never allowed once a file has staged changes
options.why: `--cached` works when the index matches either HEAD or the working tree, just not here.

options.text: Both options would lose the staged content, which exists nowhere else
options.why: The staged snapshot differs from both HEAD and disk, so only `-f` may discard it.

options.text: The working-tree file is locked by Git until the index has been refreshed
options.why: Git doesn't lock files; the message is a safety check on unique content.

options.text: Git always offers `-f` first and `--cached` only after a commit
options.why: The suggestion depends on which content would be lost, as Git's other message shows.

explanation: `git rm` refuses whenever it would destroy content you can't get back. If only the working tree differs, Git suggests `--cached` (keep your edits) or `-f`. Here three versions differ (HEAD, index and disk), so even `--cached` would throw away the unique staged snapshot, and Git only suggests `-f`. Both messages were reproduced with Git 2.55.

stem: A team is moving from Subversion to Git. Which statements describe genuine differences? (Choose two.)

options.text: A commit in Git is local until it is pushed
options.why: In SVN a commit goes straight to the central server; in Git you push separately.

options.text: Commits are identified by content hashes, not sequential revision numbers
options.why: Git IDs are hashes of the commit's content; there is no global counter like r1234.

options.text: Git requires a server connection for every commit, unlike SVN
options.why: It is the reverse: Git commits work offline, while SVN commits need the server.

options.text: Git locks files while someone edits them, the way SVN does by default
options.why: Git has no checkout locks; SVN doesn't lock by default either.

options.text: Git stores every file as a diff from the first revision
options.why: Git models commits as snapshots; deltas are only a packfile storage optimisation.

explanation: In Git every clone is a full repository: you commit locally, then share history with push and fetch. Commits are named by content hashes (SHA-1, with SHA-256 repositories available), not by a server-assigned counter. Branching and history are local operations, which changes workflows a lot compared with centralised systems.

stem: The file `docs/.gitignore` contains the single line `/tmp`. Untracked files exist at `docs/tmp/a` and `tmp/b`. Which does Git ignore?

options.text: Only `docs/tmp/a`: the slash anchors to the `docs/` directory
options.why: Patterns in a nested `.gitignore` are relative to that directory.

options.text: Only `tmp/b`: a leading slash always means the repository root
options.why: The slash anchors to the directory containing the `.gitignore`, not the root.

options.text: Both: `/tmp` matches any `tmp` directory in the project
options.why: A leading slash prevents matching at other depths.

options.text: Neither: nested `.gitignore` files can only use plain globs
options.why: Nested files support the full pattern syntax.

explanation: Each `.gitignore` is evaluated relative to its own directory, and a leading slash anchors a pattern to that directory. Git 2.55 reported `docs/.gitignore:1:/tmp` for `docs/tmp/a`, and still listed `tmp/b` as untracked.

stem:
The root `.gitignore` is:

```
!important.log
*.log
```

Is `important.log` ignored, and why?

options.text: No: negations always take priority over ordinary patterns
options.why: Priority comes from order, not from the `!`; the later line wins.

options.text: Yes: the last matching pattern wins, and `*.log` comes after the negation
options.why: Within a file Git uses the last match; put the negation after the general rule.

options.text: No: specific file names beat wildcards regardless of order
options.why: Git doesn't rank patterns by specificity, only by order and source.

options.text: Yes, but only because negations are not supported in the root `.gitignore` file
options.why: Negations work in any `.gitignore`; this is purely about order.

explanation: Within one level of precedence, the last matching pattern decides. Here `*.log` comes last and matches, so `important.log` is ignored: Git 2.55 reported `.gitignore:2:*.log`. Swapping the lines (`*.log` then `!important.log`) re-includes the file.

stem: Match each `git status --short` line with the sequence of actions that produces it.

options.text: Edited, staged with `git add`, then edited again
New file staged with `git add`, then edited again
New file staged with `git add`, then deleted from disk
Renamed with `git mv`, and nothing changed since

explanation: Read the two columns separately. The first (index vs HEAD) is M for a staged change, A for a staged new file, or R for a staged rename. The second (working tree vs index) is M if the file changed again after staging, D if it was deleted from disk, or blank if nothing changed. Each combination here was produced with Git 2.55.

stem: You are in the subdirectory `sub/` of a repository. `root.txt` (at the top level) and `sub/s.txt` are both new, untracked files. Which statements are true with Git 2.x? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git add .` stages only `sub/s.txt`
options.why: `.` is a pathspec for the current directory, so only files under `sub/` are staged.

options.text: `git add -A` stages both files, wherever you run it from
options.why: Since Git 2.0, `-A` with no pathspec operates on the whole working tree.

options.text: `git add .` stages both files, because `.` means the repository root
options.why: `.` is relative to your current directory, not the repository root.

options.text: `git add -A` stages only files under the current directory
options.why: That was Git 1.x behaviour; Git 2.x made `-A` tree-wide.

options.text: Neither command can stage files outside the current directory
options.why: `git add -A` can, and so can an explicit path such as `../root.txt`.

explanation: With Git 2.55, run from `sub/`, `git add .` staged only `sub/s.txt` and left `?? root.txt`. Then `git add -A` staged `root.txt` too. In Git 2.x, `-A` and `-u` without a pathspec apply to the whole tree, while `.` limits staging to the current directory and below.

stem: You pushed a commit, then noticed a typo in its message and ran `git commit --amend -m "Fix login redirect"`. Your next plain `git push` is rejected. Why?

options.text: The remote rejects commit messages that were edited after creation
options.why: The remote doesn't inspect messages; the problem is how the branches compare.

options.text: Amending made a new commit, so your branch no longer contains the pushed one
options.why: The remote branch isn't an ancestor of yours, so the push isn't a fast-forward.

options.text: `--amend` only works on commits that have not been staged yet
options.why: Amend works on the current HEAD commit, whether or not it was pushed.

options.text: The amended commit keeps the same hash, so Git sees nothing new that needs pushing
options.why: Amending always creates a new commit with a new hash.

explanation: A commit's hash covers its message, tree, parents and metadata, so amending creates a new commit that replaces HEAD. The remote still has the old commit, which your branch no longer contains, so a normal push isn't a fast-forward and is rejected. Only amend commits you haven't shared, or coordinate with the team and use `--force-with-lease`.
